## Phase I — The advisory war and escalation (Jan 1964 – Jul 1965)

### How the phase ends (changed)

By the end of July 1965 the advisory war is over. The decision to commit US ground forces in strength has been taken, the 173rd Airborne Brigade and the III Marine Amphibious Force are in the country, the 1st Cavalry Division (Airmobile) is preparing to sail, and Rolling Thunder is in its fifth month. On the other side, the Viet Cong have formed regiments and divisions in the provinces around Saigon and in the coastal lowlands, PAVN regular regiments are in the Central Highlands, and the summer offensive has broken ARVN battalions at Ba Gia and Dong Xoai faster than they could be rebuilt, though none of the general reserve has been wiped out. In the countryside, the Viet Cong infrastructure administers, taxes and conscripts in a large share of the hamlets, and outside the held belt the government's pacification effort has nothing like the stable administration or the local security it needs. Inside it the summer is not the historical one: about 330,000 hectares of rice land have been titled to about 270,000 families, rent is no longer paid in most of the districts the government holds, and in those districts the government's arrival no longer means the landlord's¹. Where the government does not hold the hamlets at night, nothing has changed except the promise.

In Saigon, the Thieu–Ky junta has just taken power after a year and a half of coups. In Washington, the war has an open-ended authority from Congress and a decision on troops announced without the reserves, without a tax increase and without a declaration. In Hanoi, the Politburo has committed itself to winning before the Americans arrive in strength and must now decide whether to fight them. It will: in October the PAVN regiments of the B3 Front will go after the camp at Plei Me, and the Ia Drang will follow. The war that Phase II inherits is a war between two armies that each believe they can outlast the other, fought over a population that neither government has secured.

About 1,100 village posts are settled, two-thirds of the chiefs have come from the list, and the infrastructure has begun to leave the villages around the posts². The sea route to the coast is closed and the Cambodian route open, and the enemy's rear is on the U-2S's maps while his regiments under the canopy and his cadres in the hamlets are as hidden as before. The general reserve enters Phase II weakened but whole, and the Front enters it with between 10,000 and 30,000 of the Republic's carbines³. On Guam the B-52Js hold about 1,400 measured targets in the cell's folders and authority to strike none of them in the North.

Phung Hoang ends the phase with about 140 district centres open, every one behind a settled post, and a method that has reached above the hamlet in one district on the edge of Saigon and in a dozen in the Delta⁴. About 1,100 selected advisers are in the subsectors and battalions, speaking to their counterparts without interpreters; the rest of the field posts are still held on the old tour. The Front has begun to move its district committees out of the held belt, which costs it the villages' daily obedience and gains it the safety of the contested edge.

By the end of July 1965 the board has filled about 70 of the army's roughly 190 manoeuvre battalion commands and relieved its first nine commanders; the rest are still held by men the generals put there, and about a third of all battalions are still commanded by captains, because the army is short of majors and the career-course gate makes none faster⁵. The companies are led almost everywhere by the classes of 1957–63. The generals are the generals of 1963, and every one of them has learned that the board can be bargained with and cannot be ignored.

The Directorate ends the phase with its plants at about half their capacity and the domestic share four months old; about 5,000 PF radios, 6,000 hamlet radios and 600,000 dry cells have gone to the held belt, and the Front's mines in Long An have Go Vap batteries in them⁶. Route 1 on the coast has been reopened after the worst flood in memory, and the Front has an industrial working class in Bien Hoa to organise.

The army that enters Phase II has trained every private it has enlisted for eight years, and every territorial; it has kept about 2,000–3,000 of its best sergeants at the training centres to do it, in the two years it could least spare them, and the Muster Service has caught the centres that sold the course short. The general reserve was broken at Ba Gia and Dong Xoai and came back from both with more of its men than on any course before this one; the battalions are steadier than history's by a band, though the enemy still chooses where they fight⁷.

The NCO corps that enters Phase II has been schooled for its grades for eight years, regular and territorial alike, and about 1,300–2,500 of its best sergeants are teaching at Nha Trang, the division schools and the territorial centres, on top of the drill sergeants at Quang Trung⁸. The 4th Marine Battalion at Binh Gia and the 7th Airborne at Dong Xoai were broken and came back with more of their men than on either earlier course, because their sergeants took command when their officers fell. The enemy has the academy's leader's manual and has begun to teach its local forces the ARVN platoon's routine.

The combined command ends the phase as a channel, not yet a command. It survived Khanh's coup by passing every order through his office, and it learned in its first month that operational control means what the junta of the day allows. Seoul and Canberra have consented on conditions: a Korean countersignature on every order to a Korean formation, and an Australian casualty estimate sent to Canberra. The task force ends the phase about 1,100 strong, with one campaign that found nothing for two months and then broke the Can Giuoc security section from one notebook⁹. The Hoc Mon committee that STILL WATER drove out governs from Cu Chi, and the task force's III Corps task group has its name.

### New: The combined command stands up, and Khanh's coup tests it
*1 Jan – 31 Mar 1964 · Saigon; the Joint General Staff compound and the MACV headquarters at Tan Son Nhut; the four corps headquarters at Da Nang, Pleiku, Bien Hoa and Can Tho · EV012-1*

*Initiative: allied*

The Combined Operations Command, Vietnam, was proclaimed in the same session of 1 January 1964 as the land, police and Phung Hoang decrees. It was the one decree of the session that the Military Revolutionary Council signed with visible reluctance. General Paul D. Harkins became combined commander. Lieutenant General Tran Van Don, the council's chief of the Joint General Staff, named Major General Le Van Kim as Vietnamese deputy. Kim was the general of the council most trusted in the American Mission and least trusted by the corps commanders. The Korean and Australian deputies existed on paper. Seoul sent a brigadier general with a liaison staff of eleven. Canberra appointed the commander of the Australian Army Training Team, Colonel F. P. Serong, as its interim deputy, with a staff of four⁹. In January 1964 their contingents were a Korean field hospital and Taekwondo instructors not yet arrived, and about 30 Australian advisers in the field¹⁰¹⁰.

The staff was built in a requisitioned school building on the edge of Tan Son Nhut. By the end of January it held about 260 officers: 140 American from the MACV J2, J3 and J5, 110 Vietnamese drawn from the JGS and the corps staffs, and a handful of Koreans and Australians⁹. The first combined operations order, for a sweep of the Plain of Reeds by the ARVN 7th Division with the 9th Division blocking across the IV Corps boundary, was drafted in Vietnamese and English on 22 January. It was never issued.

At dawn on 30 January Major General Nguyen Khanh, commanding I Corps, took the government. He was a corps commander under the combined commander's operational control, and he used the command's own network. The combined centre at Da Nang, still only a communications room and nine officers, passed I Corps traffic to Saigon on the night of the coup, and the American duty officer had no reason to stop it⁹. Kim was arrested with the Dalat generals that morning. For nine days the combined command had no Vietnamese deputy and no Vietnamese orders. The corps commanders took theirs from Khanh, and Harkins issued none, because there was nobody on the Vietnamese side to countersign them.

What saved the command was the same lever that saved the decrees. On 2 February the President's note to Khanh carried the Mission's condition on the decrees. Harkins and Ambassador Lodge added the combined command to it on 4 February, in a meeting at which Khanh asked how an American general could command his army. Lodge answered that the command had not been designed to command a coup and would not be used against one, and that the aid that paid the RVNAF's salaries was conditional on the command's continuing. Khanh needed the Americans more than he resented the arrangement, and he made a counter-offer. The combined command would continue, the Vietnamese deputy would be his man, Major General Nguyen Van Thieu, and Thieu would be made Khanh's own chief of staff as well, so that every combined order passed through Khanh's office before it reached a corps⁹. Harkins accepted on 9 February. The first combined order went out on 14 February, three weeks late and countersigned by a deputy whose first loyalty was to the man who had just used the command's radios to take the state.

By the end of March the command had issued eleven operations orders and had learned two things that no study had predicted. The first was that operational control meant exactly what the junta of the day wished it to mean. Under Minh it had been a concession, and under Khanh it was a channel through the prime minister's office. The second was that the Vietnamese staff officers were better than their American colleagues had expected and their orders slower. A combined order took about four days to clear Khanh's office in February and about thirty hours by late March, as Thieu learned which orders Khanh wished to see⁹. On 26 March the combined staff sent the ARVN 21st Division across the IV Corps boundary into the Ca Mau forests on a combined order in 26 hours, the first time in the war an ARVN division had moved across a corps boundary on a foreign commander's order. It found a base camp and no regiment.

### New: Operation DRY SEASON: the Can Giuoc security section
*20 Jul – 18 Dec 1964 · Can Giuoc, Can Duoc and Rach Kien Districts, Long An Province; the Rung Sat edge of Nha Be, Gia Dinh Province · EV012-2*

*Initiative: allied*

The task force's first campaign was aimed at the men who had killed the title holders of Phuoc Lai. The Long An provincial security section and the Can Giuoc district committee's armed propaganda teams had killed 37 title holders and 9 land committee members between 9 June and 14 July, and the province had suspended titling in the two districts¹. On 20 July the task force's III Corps task group, then about 180 strong, opened Operation DRY SEASON from a compound at Tan An under an American Special Forces major, Thomas R. Garvin, with a Special Branch captain, Nguyen Huu Phuoc, as his deputy⁹. Its raid element was one Special Forces detachment, a SEAL platoon of SEAL Team One on loan from the Rung Sat, and the Long An Provincial Reconnaissance Unit of about 70 men. Its lift was three UH-1Bs and two UH-1Ds of the 120th Aviation Company, kept on call at Tan Son Nhut.

The first two months produced almost nothing. The task group had the Long An Special Branch's files, six months old and built on hamlets the police held by day only. The district centre at Can Giuoc did not yet exist. Of 19 operations in August and September, 14 found the target gone, 3 took a man the magistrate at Tan An released within 72 hours, and 2 took real cadres who knew nothing of the security section. The 2026 cycle was attempted and abandoned in the same weeks. The task group's American planners ran raids two and three nights running on targets the exploitation cell had not confirmed, and the magistrate released 11 of 17 detainees in September⁹.

The turn came from a ledger. On 3 October a Rach Kien PF platoon ambushed a tax team on the canal at Long Huu and killed two men. One of them carried a notebook listing the district committee's monthly collections by hamlet, with a courier's route to the security section's base in the nipa swamps on the Nha Be edge of the Rung Sat. The exploitation cell had the notebook translated by morning. On the night of 5–6 October the SEAL platoon went up the Soai Rap in two STAB boats and a PBR borrowed from the Vietnamese Navy's river assault group. It inserted at the mouth of the Rach Ong Chuong and walked into the courier station at 0340. It took four men alive and a fifth was killed reaching for a K-50. One of the four was the security section's deputy chief, Ba Lien, who had commanded the Phuoc Lai killings. He was handed to Phuoc at Tan An at 0710 and before a magistrate on 7 October⁹.

What Ba Lien told the interrogators, and what his papers told the exploitation cell, opened the section. Over the following ten weeks the task group mounted 41 operations in Can Giuoc, Can Duoc, Rach Kien and the Nha Be edge. They took 58 people on warrant, of whom the magistrates released 19, and killed 9, two of them men whom the Commission's audit in January could not show to be cadres. Of the security section's 23 members, 14 were dead, in prison or had rallied by 18 December. Its chief had gone to the Rung Sat proper, where the task group could not follow without a battalion⁹. One PRU member and one SEAL were killed, the SEAL by a booby-trapped bunker at Ap Dong Thanh on 2 November.

Titling resumed in the eight Can Giuoc hamlets with PF posts in February 1965, two months earlier than on the course of memorandum 001. The other hamlets waited. The section was rebuilt by the spring of 1965 from cadres sent down from the Saigon–Gia Dinh Region, but the new men did not know the hamlets, and no title holder was killed in Can Giuoc in 1965⁹. DRY SEASON was a small operation that showed two things: the task force was worth nothing in its first two months, and it was worth a security section once it held one notebook.

### New: The red cards: Seoul, Canberra and the combined command
*8 Jan – 30 Jul 1965 · Seoul; Canberra; Saigon; Bien Hoa air base; Di An, Bien Hoa Province · EV012-3*

*Initiative: allied*

The Korean and Australian governments' consent to combined command, stipulated by this headquarters' instructions, was tested when their troops arrived. In Seoul the National Assembly debated the dispatch of the Dove Force of engineers and a security battalion in January 1965. The opposition asked whether Korean soldiers would be commanded by Americans abroad as they had refused to be commanded at home in matters of domestic order. President Park's defence minister, Kim Sung-eun, answered that they would be under the combined commander's operational control "for the tasks agreed between the governments and no others"⁹. That was the red card, stated in public. The Dove Force reached Di An in March under a Korean brigadier, and it took combined orders for its construction tasks without dispute, because it had no others to take¹⁰.

The Australians had already given their consent at a price. When 1st Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment arrived at Bien Hoa in June 1965 and joined the 173rd Airborne Brigade, Canberra's instructions to Brigadier O. D. Jackson, commanding Australian Army Force Vietnam, set three conditions on the combined command. The battalion would not be broken up below company level. It would not be employed in the Delta. And any operation expected to cost it more than a stated number of casualties would be referred to Canberra. The third condition was the one the combined staff had not expected. It meant that a combined order to the Australian battalion carried a casualty estimate, and that the estimate went to a capital. On 28 June, when the 173rd went into War Zone D, the combined staff's estimate for the battalion's part was sent to Canberra overnight and approved by 0600⁹. Nothing in the operation required the delay. The precedent did.

The Koreans' combat consent was the larger question, and it was settled on paper in July. The working arrangement that historically gave the Koreans MACV's support without American command (6 September 1965) was replaced here by a combined agreement of 23 July¹⁰. It placed the Korean field forces under the combined commander's operational control within an agreed area of responsibility on the II Corps coast, gave the Korean commander a right to refer any order outside that area to Seoul, and required a Korean officer to countersign any combined order to a Korean formation. Lieutenant General Chae Myung-shin signed it in Saigon. He told the combined commander, General William C. Westmoreland, that he would carry out every order he countersigned and countersign only the ones he would carry out⁹.

That sentence defined the Korean contingent for the rest of the war. It was operational control in name and a Korean veto in practice. The combined staff learned to write orders for the Korean divisions that the Korean commander had already agreed to. It was, I judge, a better arrangement than the historical one for exactly one reason: the Koreans' orders and the ARVN's now came from the same plan, so that the seam between the Korean area and the ARVN 22nd Division's was planned by one staff instead of negotiated by two⁹.

## Phase II — The main force war (Aug 1965 – Dec 1967)

### How the phase ends (changed)

At the end of 1967 the United States has about 486,000 military personnel in Vietnam and has lost 9,378 of them killed by hostile action in the year¹¹. Rolling Thunder has dropped about 864,000 tons on North Vietnam by the Pentagon's announcement of 31 December¹², and the North's air defences have made every strike near Hanoi expensive. The Trail is carrying more than ever; truck movements rise sharply from October to December. The enemy order of battle is in dispute: MACV counts about 300,000 communist personnel, the CIA up to 430,000¹³, and the disagreement turns on whether the guerrillas and the political infrastructure, the part of the enemy the main-force war does not touch, are counted at all.

On 21 November Westmoreland tells the National Press Club that the enemy is "unable to mount a major offensive" and that "the end begins to come into view"¹³. The administration's progress campaign of the autumn rests on the body count, the Hamlet Evaluation System and the claim that the crossover point is near. McNamara, who has lost confidence in the war, has announced his departure for the World Bank, and Johnson's offer at San Antonio on 29 September, to stop the bombing in exchange for prompt and productive talks, has been rejected by Hanoi. In Saigon there is, for the first time since 1963, an elected government under Thieu, and in the countryside CORDS has begun to organize the territorial war, from a less low base than history's. About 820,000 hectares have been titled to about 640,000 families, rent has ended in law and largely in fact wherever the government holds the night, and the Commission has convicted a general. The infrastructure of the Front is smaller in the Delta than on the historical course, and its tax take lower, but it is intact in every hamlet the government does not hold after dark, and those hamlets are still most of the contested countryside¹.

In Hanoi the decision is taken. The PAVN and VC main forces have been drawn to the borders and have drawn the Americans after them; the VC's local forces and cadres in and around the cities are preparing; and the Politburo has set the Tet holiday of 1968 as the moment for the General Offensive and General Uprising. The phase ends with each side certain that the other is weaker than it is, and with the population of the South, the object of the war, still largely outside the reach of either army's strategy.

In the held belt the resident infrastructure has been driven out of most villages with settled posts by the end of 1967, and the arrest count has fallen because there is little left there to arrest². The National Police numbers about 80,000, the chiefs have mostly held their districts for two or three years, and the Front's legal cadres are in the towns, where the police knows less.

The enemy's external supply is measured: the Trail by the panhandle watch, Sihanoukville by the count, the North's roads by the Gulf watch, and every measure says that what arrives exceeds what the South's forces need from the North¹⁴. That knowledge is honest from 1965 rather than from 1970, and it has not changed the rules, the bombing or the strategy. Its main effect on Washington has been to deliver bad news early.

The RVNAF enters 1968 with the rifles it has carried for four years and a Regional Force that the corps commanders want for their own operations, bound since 1967 by the rule that keeps it in its provinces. The American army has had no rifle crisis and no inquiry, and has lost somewhat fewer men in the first minutes of its fights; it is the same army in every other respect, fighting the same battles on the enemy's terms.

The bombers have learned two things in two years: that a bridge they can measure dies in a night and is replaced by five crossings they cannot, and that a siege they can measure becomes the enemy's worst battle. The second lesson is the one the headquarters remembers going into 1968.

Phung Hoang has a centre in every district and an audited count of about 18,000 neutralized since 1965, about one in five of them members of district or village committees, and the Front's district administration in the held belt now governs from the contested edge by courier. The word Phoenix has been a press story since March 1967. About 7,000 selected advisers hold every field post below corps; the American battalions have changed over once or twice each as units, have fought better in the contacts they were granted, and have learned at Dien Ban to keep their reliefs off the dark of the moon. The staggered six-week overlap that followed raised the peak American strength in theater by about 15,000–25,000 men, which the expansion battalions of 1967 waited for, so that the enemy's tactic against the relief was paid for in American spaces rather than American dead⁴. None of it has changed who chooses the battle.

The ARVN ends 1967 with about four in five of its battalions commanded by officers the board chose, on eighteen-month commands, with the captain-led battalion nearly gone and the thirty-day review feared and read; about a third fewer of its battalions have been rendered ineffective in 1966–67 than on the historical course, which no report shows because the enemy declined the fights that would have shown it⁵. The 25th Division has a commander from the list and the corps have the commanders they had. The Military Security Service has its first file on the board's officers as a political factor, and COSVN has had every list the board published.

The factories end 1967 producing what the domestic share buys, with the steelworks short of power and the arsenal short of its gunners' trust after Phu Cat. Every post of the held belt has a radio, the Front attacks those that can call about a third less often than those that cannot, and where the guns can reach the posts the first call is for fire⁶. The posts hold themselves better than the hamlets around them.

The ARVN ends 1967 trained to the man; training alone would have left it as short of squad leaders as history's, and what filled most of the empty slots was the NCO schooling described below; its battalions have lost about a tenth to a sixth fewer men in the ambushes the enemy still lays, beyond what the rifles and the officers saved, and about one in eight fewer battalions has been broken in 1966–67 than the officer reforms alone would have left. The drill-sergeant corps has begun to return about 650–1,800 platoon sergeants a year to the battalions⁷. In the lowlands of Quang Nam and Quang Ngai the mine has replaced the firefight as the enemy's way of killing Americans, and in the districts around Saigon the Front's guerrilla squads are drilled by men the Republic trained.

The ARVN ends 1967 with its squads and platoons led by schooled men: about two in three of the slots the field commissions emptied are held by corporals first class who passed the leader's course, and the squads of the 7th Division held their base of fire at Hau My when their officers fell. I judge that about one in six to one in five fewer ARVN battalions were broken in 1966–67 than the officer reforms and the basic course alone would have left, and that the posts of the Delta lost about a tenth to a fifth fewer to night attack than the radio and the trained platoon had already saved⁸. None of it shows in a return: the enemy attacked less what kept its routine. American sergeants pass the Basic Leader Course at Bien Hoa or wait for it, and the waiver of 1966 has become a ninety-day deferral.

The combined command ends 1967 with one corps area under a Vietnamese commander and three under American deputies who in practice run them, a quarterly plan the corps commanders execute at their own speed, and a two-layer plan that protects its operations and insults its Vietnamese staff. The task force has broken the Front's district government of the Saigon belt from its edge: the Hoc Mon committee and the region's finance section govern from the Ho Bo woods, and the region's collections from the posted villages are about an eighth of 1964's⁹. On the II Corps coast it has a list it abandoned and a story the Front still tells.

> At the end of 1967 the United States has about 486,000 military personnel in Vietnam and has lost 9,378 of them killed by hostile action in the year¹¹. Rolling Thunder has dropped about 864,000 tons on North Vietnam by the Pentagon's announcement of 31 December¹², and the North's air defences have made every strike near Hanoi expensive. The Trail is carrying more than ever; truck movements rise sharply from October to December. The enemy order of battle is in dispute: MACV counts about 300,000 communist personnel, the CIA up to 430,000, and the disagreement turns on whether the guerrillas and the political infrastructure, the part of the enemy the main-force war does not touch, are counted at all.

> On 21 November Westmoreland tells the National Press Club that the enemy is "unable to mount a major offensive" and that "the end begins to come into view"¹³. The administration's progress campaign of the autumn rests on the body count, the Hamlet Evaluation System and the claim that the crossover point is near. McNamara, who has lost confidence in the war, has announced his departure for the World Bank, and Johnson's offer at San Antonio on 29 September, to stop the bombing in exchange for prompt and productive talks, has been rejected by Hanoi. In Saigon there is, for the first time since 1963, an elected government under Thieu, and in the countryside CORDS has begun to organize the territorial war, from a less low base than history's. About 820,000 hectares have been titled to about 640,000 families, rent has ended in law and largely in fact wherever the government holds the night, and the Commission has convicted a general. The infrastructure of the Front is smaller in the Delta than on the historical course, and its tax take lower, but it is intact in every hamlet the government does not hold after dark, and those hamlets are still most of the contested countryside¹.
> 
> In Hanoi the decision is taken. The PAVN and VC main forces have been drawn to the borders and have drawn the Americans after them; the VC's local forces and cadres in and around the cities are preparing; and the Politburo has set the Tet holiday of 1968 as the moment for the General Offensive and General Uprising. The phase ends with each side certain that the other is weaker than it is, and with the population of the South, the object of the war, still largely outside the reach of either army's strategy.
> 
> In the held belt the resident infrastructure has been driven out of most villages with settled posts by the end of 1967, and the arrest count has fallen because there is little left there to arrest². The National Police numbers about 80,000, the chiefs have mostly held their districts for two or three years, and the Front's legal cadres are in the towns, where the police knows less.
> 
> The enemy's external supply is measured: the Trail by the panhandle watch, Sihanoukville by the count, the North's roads by the Gulf watch, and every measure says that what arrives exceeds what the South's forces need from the North¹⁴. That knowledge is honest from 1965 rather than from 1970, and it has not changed the rules, the bombing or the strategy. Its main effect on Washington has been to deliver bad news early.
> 
> The RVNAF enters 1968 with the rifles it has carried for four years and a Regional Force that the corps commanders want for their own operations, bound since 1967 by the rule that keeps it in its provinces. The American army has had no rifle crisis and no inquiry, and has lost somewhat fewer men in the first minutes of its fights; it is the same army in every other respect, fighting the same battles on the enemy's terms.
> 
> The bombers have learned two things in two years: that a bridge they can measure dies in a night and is replaced by five crossings they cannot, and that a siege they can measure becomes the enemy's worst battle. The second lesson is the one the headquarters remembers going into 1968.
> 
> Phung Hoang has a centre in every district and an audited count of about 18,000 neutralized since 1965, about one in five of them members of district or village committees, and the Front's district administration in the held belt now governs from the contested edge by courier. The word Phoenix has been a press story since March 1967. About 7,000 selected advisers hold every field post below corps; the American battalions have changed over once or twice each as units, have fought better in the contacts they were granted, and have learned at Dien Ban to keep their reliefs off the dark of the moon. The staggered six-week overlap that followed raised the peak American strength in theater by about 15,000–25,000 men, which the expansion battalions of 1967 waited for, so that the enemy's tactic against the relief was paid for in American spaces rather than American dead⁴. None of it has changed who chooses the battle.
> 
> The ARVN ends 1967 with about four in five of its battalions commanded by officers the board chose, on eighteen-month commands, with the captain-led battalion nearly gone and the thirty-day review feared and read; about a third fewer of its battalions have been rendered ineffective in 1966–67 than on the historical course, which no report shows because the enemy declined the fights that would have shown it⁵. The 25th Division has a commander from the list and the corps have the commanders they had. The Military Security Service has its first file on the board's officers as a political factor, and COSVN has had every list the board published.
> 
> The factories end 1967 producing what the domestic share buys, with the steelworks short of power and the arsenal short of its gunners' trust after Phu Cat. Every post of the held belt has a radio, the Front attacks those that can call about a third less often than those that cannot, and where the guns can reach the posts the first call is for fire⁶. The posts hold themselves better than the hamlets around them.
> 
> The ARVN ends 1967 trained to the man; training alone would have left it as short of squad leaders as history's, and what filled most of the empty slots was the NCO schooling described below; its battalions have lost about a tenth to a sixth fewer men in the ambushes the enemy still lays, beyond what the rifles and the officers saved, and about one in eight fewer battalions has been broken in 1966–67 than the officer reforms alone would have left. The drill-sergeant corps has begun to return about 650–1,800 platoon sergeants a year to the battalions⁷. In the lowlands of Quang Nam and Quang Ngai the mine has replaced the firefight as the enemy's way of killing Americans, and in the districts around Saigon the Front's guerrilla squads are drilled by men the Republic trained.
> 
> The ARVN ends 1967 with its squads and platoons led by schooled men: about two in three of the slots the field commissions emptied are held by corporals first class who passed the leader's course, and the squads of the 7th Division held their base of fire at Hau My when their officers fell. I judge that about one in six to one in five fewer ARVN battalions were broken in 1966–67 than the officer reforms and the basic course alone would have left, and that the posts of the Delta lost about a tenth to a fifth fewer to night attack than the radio and the trained platoon had already saved⁸. None of it shows in a return: the enemy attacked less what kept its routine. American sergeants pass the Basic Leader Course at Bien Hoa or wait for it, and the waiver of 1966 has become a ninety-day deferral.

### New: Operation FOLLOW THROUGH
*2 Aug 1965 – 30 Jun 1966 · Cu Chi and Trang Bang Districts, Hau Nghia Province; Hoc Mon District, Gia Dinh Province; the Ho Bo and Boi Loi woods and the Filhol rubber, Binh Duong Province · EV012-4*

*Initiative: allied*

FOLLOW THROUGH was the task force's answer to the district committee that STILL WATER had driven out of Hoc Mon. Five of the Hoc Mon committee's 14 members had escaped STILL WATER and governed the district's posted villages from Cu Chi by courier⁴. With them in the Cu Chi hamlets along the Saigon River sat the Saigon–Gia Dinh Region's finance and economy section, which collected taxes from the market gardens of Hoc Mon and Go Vap and the rubber workers of the Filhol plantation. On 2 August 1965 the III Corps task group opened the operation from Hoc Mon district town, with Major Garvin commanding and Lieutenant Colonel Phuoc of the Special Branch as his deputy. The task group was now about 420 strong, with a Special Forces detachment, two SEAL platoons, the Gia Dinh and Hau Nghia PRUs and four UH-1Ds and two UH-1B gunships of its own⁹.

The operation ran on the cycle the task force had learned in Long An: an arrest or a rallier, exploitation the same morning, the follow-on that night. Its first two months took eleven of the region finance section's couriers and none of its members, because every courier carried only the next courier's name. The break was a woman again, as it had been in STILL WATER. On 14 October a 23-year-old cashier of the finance section, arrested at a market stall in Hoc Mon with 41,000 piasters in a rice sack, rallied on the 16th against a named offer that her mother would not be detained. She described the section's three meeting houses in An Nhon Tay and Phu Hoa Dong⁹.

The raid on Phu Hoa Dong on the night of 19–20 October was the task force's first contested-belt operation at full scale. Two SEAL platoons and the Gia Dinh PRU inserted by helicopter at 0230 into a paddy east of the hamlet. A Regional Forces company of Cu Chi district held a cordon on the river side, and a company of the ARVN 25th Division's 49th Regiment closed the land side. The III Corps combined centre had tasked that company at 1500 the previous afternoon on the task group's request, against the division's own plan for the night. The team took the section's deputy chief and two cadres alive in a tunnel entrance under a family altar, with the section's ledger for the first nine months of 1965. One SEAL was killed by a grenade thrown from a second tunnel mouth. The PRU killed three men in the paddy who had fired on the cordon. One of them was the deputy chief's 16-year-old son, carrying a K-44 rifle⁹.

The ledger was the most valuable document the task force had yet taken. It recorded the region's tax collections hamlet by hamlet across Hoc Mon, Go Vap, Cu Chi and Trang Bang, and it named the collectors. Between November 1965 and March 1966 the task group made 64 arrests on warrants drawn from it, of which the magistrates released 21. It killed 17 people in raids, of whom the Commission's audit of May 1966 could show 13 to be cadres and could not show 4. Of the Hoc Mon committee's five surviving members, three were taken and one rallied. The fifth, the committee's secretary, Nguyen Van Tu, left Cu Chi for the Ho Bo woods in January 1966 with the finance section's remaining members, as the American 25th Infantry Division arrived at Cu Chi and began clearing the plantation edge⁹. The task group could not follow him there. The woods were the 165th VC Regiment's base area and a main-force problem.

What FOLLOW THROUGH achieved shows in the Front's own accounts. The region finance section's collections from the posted villages of Hoc Mon and Go Vap in the first half of 1966 were about one-eighth of the first half of 1964's, against about one-fifth on the course of memorandum 006. Its collections from Cu Chi's contested hamlets fell by about two-fifths, where on that course they had grown. Nobody governed Hoc Mon from Cu Chi after March 1966. The Front governed it from the Ho Bo woods, eighteen kilometres further out, by couriers who now took two nights rather than one, and it never re-established a tax collector who lived in a Hoc Mon hamlet before 1968⁹. The operation cost the task force two SEALs, four PRU members and a Regional Forces soldier killed. It cost the Front the region's tax administration west of Saigon for about a year. It cost the families of the four men the audit could not clear a reason to hate the government, and the census told the Front which families they were.

### New: The II Corps list and its abandonment
*15 Nov 1965 – 2 Apr 1966 · Tuy An and Song Cau Districts, Phu Yen Province; Phu My and Phu Cat Districts, Binh Dinh Province; Qui Nhon · EV012-5*

*Initiative: both*

The II Corps task group was formed at Qui Nhon in November 1965, as the ROK Capital Division settled into its area around Qui Nhon and Phu Cat¹⁰. It worked on thinner ground than any other. The coastal districts of Binh Dinh and Phu Yen had been the Viet Minh's Interzone V for nine years and the Front's since 1960, and the Special Branch held files on hamlets it had never entered at night. The district centres opened there in 1965 had little but ralliers' accounts. The task group's commander, an American lieutenant colonel, Harold J. Beck, adopted in December what the 2026 task forces had called a high-value target list: 64 named members of the Phu Yen and Binh Dinh province committees, to be captured or, if they resisted, killed⁹. Its raid elements were a Special Forces detachment, a Korean special-forces team of the 1st Airborne Special Forces Group attached to the Capital Division, and the two provinces' PRUs.

Military Region 5 had its own plans for the coast, made for its own reasons. Its Party Committee had decided in October 1965 to hold the 2nd VC Regiment and the 3rd PAVN Division's regiments in the An Lao, Kim Son and Suoi Ca valleys through the dry season of 1966. One reason was to protect the rice harvest of the coastal plain, on which its own forces lived. The other was that it refused the B3 Front's request to send a regiment to the Highlands. The region's leaders held that the coast, not the plateau, was the decisive ground of their war⁹. That rivalry between two of Hanoi's commands kept a division on the Binh Dinh coast through the winter, and it kept the province committees close to the regiments that protected them.

<!-- initiative -->
The list was worked from January to March 1966. It produced 11 operations, 9 detainees and 14 dead. Three of the dead were on the list. On the night of 19–20 January the Korean team and the Phu Yen PRU raided a house in Hoa Thanh village, Tuy An District, on a rallier's word that the Phu Yen committee's security chief slept there. They killed four men who ran from the house and found no papers. The Commission's inspectors, who reached Tuy An on 3 February, found that the four were a family who had sheltered a cadre once, two years before, and that the rallier had a land dispute with them. Under the 1964 police statute a killing without a warrant was a matter for the magistrate. On 16 February the Phu Yen magistrate referred two members of the Korean team for homicide, and the Korean commander refused to surrender them⁹. Chae Myung-shin's position was that his soldiers answered to Korean military law and nobody else's. The Phu Yen province committee's position was a leaflet, in every market from Tuy Hoa to Song Cau within the week, naming the four men and the Korean unit.

On 2 April the combined commander and the task force commander ended the list in II Corps. The Korean team was withdrawn from the task force at Seoul's request, the American team was kept, and the II Corps task group returned to warrant arrests in the held towns of the coast and named offers in the contested districts. The episode cost the task force its credibility in Phu Yen for two years and gave the Front its first story about it. It was a year earlier than the Duc Thanh raid that made "Phoenix" a press word, and it was believed on the coast where the Duc Thanh story was not. The two Korean soldiers were tried by a Korean court-martial in Seoul in 1967 and acquitted⁹.

### New: The Delta corps
*1 Jul 1966 – 31 Dec 1967 · Can Tho, Phong Dinh Province; Dinh Tuong and Kien Hoa Provinces; Dong Tam base, Dinh Tuong Province · EV012-6*

*Initiative: allied*

On 1 July 1966 the IV Corps combined centre passed to Vietnamese command. The ARVN IV Corps commander, Major General Dang Van Quang, became the combined commander's subordinate for the Delta, with the American senior adviser in IV Corps, a brigadier general, as his deputy⁹. It was the first time in the war that an American officer served as deputy to a Vietnamese commander in a chain of command rather than as his adviser. Quang was the President's choice for the corps, not the board's, and among the most corrupt generals in the army by the account of every American who served with him. The combined command could not choose him. It could only command through him or ask for his relief, and in July 1966 it did not ask.

The arrangement worked on paper for four months and in practice for about one. Quang ran the IV Corps combined centre as he ran the corps: the plans were written by his staff and the American deputy's together, and executed by divisions whose commanders reported to Quang, and through him to the palace, before they reported to the combined centre. When Quang was removed in November 1966 in the palace's own reshuffle, his successor, Major General Nguyen Van Manh, kept the arrangement. Manh was honest and cautious. Under him the Delta's combined orders went out on time and were executed slowly⁹.

The test of the one-in-three rule came in June 1967. The American 9th Infantry Division's 2nd Brigade, with the Navy's Mobile Riverine Force, began operations from Dong Tam in Dinh Tuong in the spring of 1967. In June its commander asked the IV Corps combined centre for two battalions of the ARVN 7th Division to block for the riverine force's sweep of the Cam Son base area. Both battalions were assigned to territorial security in Cai Lay and Cai Be, and they were the reaction force for the posts whose first call was for fire⁶. Manh refused the second battalion under the rule, and the American deputy supported him against the division commander. The sweep went in on 19 June with one ARVN battalion blocking. Part of the 263rd VC Main Force Battalion slipped east through the gap the second battalion would have held⁹. No post in Cai Lay fell that month.

At the end of 1967 the combined headquarters judged the Delta corps a qualified success. The Vietnamese commander had commanded the combined system for eighteen months, the corps staff had written every combined order in the Delta, and the American deputy had overruled nothing. Two things were also true. The Delta divisions' plans were Manh's caution written down. And the American brigade in the Delta, under its own division commander, had fought its own war in the Plain of Reeds and the Cam Son as though the combined command did not exist, because its division commander answered to a field force before he answered to the corps⁹. The combined command did not hand over a second corps in 1967. The handover the transfer needed had begun, and it was proceeding at the speed of the generals the palace chose.

## Phase III — Tet and its aftermath (Jan 1968 – Dec 1968)

### How the phase ends (changed)

At the end of 1968 the war has changed shape without changing direction. The VC in the South have lost much of their main and local forces and many of their cadres in the three offensives, and their recruitment has collapsed; the main-force war is now predominantly a PAVN war, and the parallel administration in the hamlets, though intact in much of the country, is under more pressure than at any time since 1959. The government in Saigon has survived Tet, mobilized, and begun with CORDS to push into the countryside; ARVN units fought better in February than anyone expected, though they remain dependent on American firepower and logistics. Against these gains, the United States has decided not to escalate further and to seek a negotiated way out; the bombing of the North has ended; and the American public's tolerance for casualties, measured in a year in which 14,592 Americans died by hostile action, has been spent¹¹.

In Hanoi, the leadership has paid heavily for the General Offensive and turned back to protracted war for the moment, but has won what it most needed: an American president who will not reinforce and a successor committed to withdrawal. The Paris talks exist; the shape of the table is being settled. Phase IV opens with a new administration in Washington, a war in the countryside that the South is better placed to fight than it has been for years, and an American army whose withdrawal is now a matter of timing.

In this war the countryside is better placed than that. About 900,000 hectares have been titled, the Front's Delta recruitment has fallen from a lower base, and its Delta battalions are filling with northerners earlier¹. The American decision of 1968 is unchanged, and so is its timing.

The National Police numbers about 95,000 and the Special Branch has buried its first constables of the Tet battles; the infrastructure in the held belt is weaker than anywhere since 1959, and every file it keeps is now held under a destruction plan².

The enemy's rear enters Phase IV counted: the surge after the halt is measured, the first dry season of Commando Hunt is scored against the radar as well as the claims¹⁴, and the American decision of 1968 is unchanged by any of it.

The RVNAF ends 1968 larger and armed throughout with weapons the historical one was still waiting for; its new territorials have rifles and too few sergeants³. The gap the rearmament opened over history is now closing from the historical side, as the M16 reaches the ARVN in 1968 and the territorials in 1969.

The PAVN leaves 1968 having learned that it does not lay siege to a position the Americans can measure; that is the one way of choosing its battles it has lost¹⁵. It chooses all the others. The panhandle is harder to cut than history's, because the bombers taught its engineers how.

Phung Hoang enters 1969 with five years of files, an audited count the press has learned to quote, and no quotas; the Front's Delta committees have lost a third of the leaders they sent into the towns⁴. The Hue district files have shown what the national file would be worth to the enemy. The selected advisers are in every field post, the first of them on their second tours, and the American battalions have fought the year as units.

The ARVN's battalions come out of 1968 with commanders who have held them through Tet and a board that has not stopped working; the mobilization's platoons have lieutenants who were sergeants and squads that have no sergeants⁵. COSVN has opened a campaign among the officers the board passed over, and the Military Security Service has a second file on the board's officers, this time as targets.

The RVNAF ends 1968 with the mobilization's soldiers trained to the same standard as the regulars of 1957, and about a month late in the field for it; the People's Self-Defense Force, which no course reached, has paid for the difference in Hau Nghia, Long An and Dinh Tuong. About 2,150 rather than 2,300 ARVN soldiers died in the first wave, and the hospitals of both armies are full of men who would have died on the historical course and are alive without a leg⁷.

The RVNAF ends 1968 with its new platoons led, in about fourteen cases in fifteen, by a man who has passed the leader's course, against about four in five on the course of memorandum 009 and about two in three historically⁸. The academy's course is four weeks for the duration and its field week intact. The posts of Cai Lay held Tet by not being attacked.

The combined command ends 1968 with a traitor found in its plans cell and the two-layer plan extended to every corps, and with one battle, Hue, fought under one commander and ended five days early⁹. The task force's work of 1965–67 showed at Tet on one road: the columns that came through Hoc Mon came through hamlets with no resident cadres to quarter or guide them. The infrastructure lost at Tet fell on a network already broken in the held belt, and the Front's district committees enter 1969 governing from further out than history's.

### New: Tet without guides in Hoc Mon
*30 Jan – 4 Feb 1968 · Hoc Mon and Go Vap Districts, Gia Dinh Province; the approaches to Tan Son Nhut from Ba Queo and Vinh Loc · EV012-8*

*Initiative: enemy*

The battalions that attacked Saigon from the northwest at Tet came down the corridor the Hoc Mon committee had governed until 1965. They passed through Hoc Mon and Go Vap to the Ba Queo crossroads and the west side of Tan Son Nhut. Historically they were guided through it by the district's infrastructure, which had hidden weapons in the hamlets for months, quartered the assault troops in the market gardens on the night of the 29th and walked them to their start lines. In this war the Hoc Mon committee had governed from the Ho Bo woods since 1966, and its tax collectors had not lived in a Hoc Mon hamlet since. The Saigon–Gia Dinh Region gave the guiding of the northwestern columns to cadres sent in from Cu Chi in December 1967. They knew the roads and not the hamlets⁹.

Three things followed, and they were small. First, the weapons. Of the nine caches the region had placed in Hoc Mon's hamlets for the assault, the task force's III Corps task group had found three in December from a courier's notebook. It read them as the stocks of a local offensive against the district towns, not of a general offensive against the capital, and passed them to the combined estimate in those words. The warning did not change the surprise of 31 January, because nobody in Saigon read three caches in one district as the city's attack. But two companies of the northwestern columns reached their start lines short of their B-40 rockets⁹.

Second, the night of the 29th. Without resident cadres to quarter them, the assault companies spent the night of 29–30 January in the open fields west of Ba Queo instead of in houses. A PF platoon at Tan Thoi Nhi, the hamlet where STILL WATER had taken the security section in 1965, saw them at 2100 on the 30th and reported a company moving south. The report reached the district at 2140 and the combined III Corps centre at 2350. At 0100 the centre put the ARVN Airborne battalion standing by at Tan Son Nhut on half an hour's notice, two hours before the attack. That was not enough to change what happened at the west gate, and it is not a claim that it did⁹.

Third, the attack's timing. The northwestern columns, guided by men who did not know the hamlets' paths, reached Tan Son Nhut's western perimeter about one to two hours later than the region's plan, after the attacks on the city's centre had begun and the base was awake. The fight at the west gate and Ba Queo was the fight of the historical record, which the base's defenders and the 3rd Squadron, 4th Cavalry won by the afternoon of the 31st. The local cost to the attackers was higher. I put the dead of the two battalions at about a sixth above the historical count, on the evidence of the fields they crossed in daylight on the 31st⁹.

The event does not change Tet. It shows on one road what the attack on the infrastructure had done by 1968: the enemy could still assemble a battalion and send it to a gate, but no longer from inside the hamlets it passed through. A committee that governs from a wood eighteen kilometres away cannot hide a rocket in a market garden.

### Changed: The battle of Hue
*31 Jan – 27 Feb 1968 · Hue, Thua Thien Province · EV000-44*

*Initiative: enemy*
In the early hours of 31 January the PAVN 4th, 5th and 6th Regiments with the 1st, 2nd and 12th Sapper Battalions, under a Hue City Front command, took almost all of Hue, the old imperial capital, except the ARVN 1st Division headquarters in the northeast corner of the Citadel and the MACV advisory compound south of the Perfume River. Brigadier General Ngo Quang Truong held his headquarters with his staff and the Hac Bao Reconnaissance Company, and brought in the 3rd Regiment, the 4th Battalion, 2nd Regiment, the 1st Airborne Task Force (2nd and 7th Airborne Battalions), Vietnamese Marine Task Force A, the 7th Armored Cavalry Squadron and the 21st and 39th Ranger Battalions. The PAVN reinforced with the 7th Battalion, 29th Regiment of the 325C Division from Khe Sanh, the 803rd Regiment and a battalion of the 90th Regiment of the 324B Division, and the 6th Battalion, 24th Regiment of the 304th Division¹⁶.

South of the river the 1st Battalion, 1st Marines and the 1st and 2nd Battalions, 5th Marines of Task Force X-Ray cleared the new city block by block, house by house, in rain and low cloud that restricted air support for most of the battle. Outside the city the 3rd Brigade of the 1st Cavalry Division, with the 2nd Battalion, 12th Cavalry, the 5th Battalion, 7th Cavalry and the 2nd Battalion, 501st Infantry, fought to cut the PAVN routes in from the west; historically it did not reach the Citadel's west wall until 25 February¹⁶. Historically the ARVN and the Marines retook the Citadel, the flag of the Front came down from its tower on 24 February, and the battle was declared over on 2 March.

In this war Hue was one battle under one commander, and it ended about five days earlier. Historically it was three battles. Truong's division fought in the Citadel, the Marines fought south of the river under their own chain, and the 1st Cavalry Division's brigade fought to the west under the Army's, with no commander below Saigon over all three until MACV Forward was established at Phu Bai on 9 February. Here the I Corps combined centre at Da Nang, under Lieutenant General Hoang Xuan Lam with Lieutenant General Robert E. Cushman of III Marine Amphibious Force as his deputy, named Truong commander of the battle of Hue at 1100 on 1 February. Brigadier General Foster C. LaHue of Task Force X-Ray became his deputy for the south bank, and the 3rd Brigade's commander became his deputy for the western approaches. One fire-support coordination centre in the Citadel took every call for naval gunfire, Marine and Army artillery and the aircraft the weather allowed, from Vietnamese and American units alike, through the switchboard the combined command had run in I Corps since 1966⁹.

The change that shortened the battle was in the west. Truong's first request to the combined centre, on the afternoon of 1 February, was for the western routes to be cut before anything else, because the PAVN was reinforcing through La Chu and the hamlets of Thon Que Chu. It was the reinforcement, not the walls, that would make the Citadel long. The combined centre gave the 3rd Brigade first call on the I Corps helicopter lift from 2 February and placed the ARVN 1st Division's 3rd Regiment under the brigade's command for the block. Historically the brigade was short of lift and fought its way overland from PK-17. The brigade reached the Citadel's west wall on 20 February rather than 25 February. The 803rd Regiment's battalion from the 324B Division, which historically entered the city through La Chu in mid-February, was caught in the open at Thon La Chu on 12–13 February by the brigade and the ARVN 3rd Regiment together, with naval gunfire from the cruiser and destroyers of the gunfire support group off the coast, called through the Citadel's centre, and broken. The flag of the Front came down from the Citadel tower on 19 February, and the combined command declared the battle over on 27 February⁹. The weather and the walls still set most of the battle's length, and nothing in the combined command touched either.

The squad weapons made Hue somewhat less costly to retake and no shorter. On the first night the Hac Bao company held the 1st Division compound with M4A1s and four squad guns against the 800th and 802nd Battalions' assault teams, where historically it held with M16s it had only recently received; the difference was small, because the Hac Bao was among the few ARVN units historically re-armed by then. Across the river the Marines fought the street battle with two or three M249s in each squad and a marksman with an M110A2 who, in a city where the PAVN held the upper floors and the far side of every street, could put rounds into a window at 200 metres from cover that a squad's rifles could not reach. The 2nd Battalion, 5th Marines' after-action report credited its marksmen with most of the PAVN machine gunners killed on the treasury and the public health building between 4 and 6 February. What took the blocks was what took them historically: the 106mm recoilless rifles, the Ontos, tear gas and men going through walls. The weather, the Citadel's walls and the PAVN's reinforcement from the west set the length of the battle, and the rifles touched none of them. I put the ARVN dead at about 410 and the American at about 215, against 458 and 250 historically³. With the battle about five days shorter and the western reinforcement broken at La Chu, I put them at about 370 and 200 in this war, and the city's destruction a little less in the Citadel's western quarter, which was the last to be cleared⁹.

The ARVN lost 458 killed and about 2,700 wounded, and the Americans 250 killed and 1,554 wounded, on the historical course. PAVN and VC dead are given from 1,042 to more than 5,000, by source. Between 5,800 and 8,000 civilians died and the city was largely destroyed. During their occupation the PAVN and VC rounded up officials, officers, priests, teachers, foreigners and others on prepared lists; after the battle mass graves were found, and more than 2,000 people are known to have been executed, with the most cited count of bodies recovered at about 2,800¹⁶. Hue was the only city the offensive held for more than a few days, and the killings there hardened the urban population of the South against the Front for the rest of the war. The five days the combined command saved were not days on which the security sections' killing stopped. Most of the executions were carried out in the first two weeks, and the shorter battle saved, I judge, a few hundred of the city's civilian dead at most, from the shelling of the western quarter rather than from the lists⁹.

In this war the battle is the same battle, and the killings are worse in one particular. The Front's Hue city security section drew its lists in this war from three sources it did not have on the historical course: a copy of the Hue family census taken from the provincial identity office through an agent in its records room in 1967, the knowledge of the Struggle Movement's student leaders who had gone to the Front after the repression of 1966, and the names of the constables and Special Branch officers of Thua Thien, which the census itself recorded by household. The teams that went through Phu Cam, Gia Hoi and the streets around the Citadel in February went to houses, not to neighbourhoods. Of the dead identified in the graves found in 1968–69, police officers, constables, census clerks and their families were about a fifth on this course, against a smaller share on the historical one. I do not raise the total. I cannot show that more people were killed, only that the lists were better and the choice of whom to kill more exact; the Mission's count of the dead is the historical count, and it is a floor².

The consequence was immediate in the Directorate. On 9 March 1968 Loan's deputy issued the order that this headquarters had urged in 1964 and the Directorate had deferred: every district and province office was to hold its census copies, informant cards and Special Branch files under a destruction plan, with thermite charges and a rehearsal every quarter². In the provinces the plan was rehearsed. Whether it would be carried out on the day it was needed was a question for another year.

The Thua Thien province centre was in the province headquarters south of the river, which the attackers held from 31 January until the 2nd Battalion, 5th Marines retook it on 6 February¹⁶. Its informant cards were not in the attackers' hands. The PIOCC's chief, Major Ton That Dinh Lang, had kept the cards of the province's 340 informants in a single safe, against Hieu's rule, because he did not trust his district centres' security; when the attack reached the compound wall at about 0330 on 31 January he burned the cards in the safe with a can of gasoline and was killed an hour later on the stairs. The district centres of Huong Thuy and Phu Vang, outside the city, kept their copies and lost them when their offices were overrun on 31 January and 1 February; the Hue city security section's lists for the southern suburbs included about 60 informants and centre staff named from those files, of whom about 40 were among the dead found in the graves at Phu Thu and Da Mai Creek⁴. The national file in Saigon, which held every one of those names, was never in danger in 1968. It was the first time the record showed what a fused file was worth to the enemy, and the destruction order of 9 March was written with the Huong Thuy file in front of it.

### New: The attack on the combined headquarters
*31 Jan – 3 Feb 1968 · The Combined Operations Command compound and the Joint General Staff compound, Tan Son Nhut, Saigon · EV012-7*

*Initiative: enemy*

At 0320 on 31 January a sapper company and a local-force battalion of the Saigon–Gia Dinh sub-regions attacked the Combined Operations Command compound on the northern edge of Tan Son Nhut, at the same hour as the attacks on the Joint General Staff compound, the air base's west gate and the embassy. The compound was held by the combined headquarters security battalion, a mixed unit of a Vietnamese military police company, an American military police company and a Korean security platoon. Its perimeter held. The sappers breached the outer wire at the vehicle gate and were stopped at the inner wall by the American company's M60s and two M113s of the Vietnamese company, and by 0700 the attack had broken into the paddy north of the base. Eleven of the compound's defenders were killed, five Vietnamese, five American and one Korean, and about 40 attackers' bodies were counted on the wire, a count I accept because the bodies lay inside the compound's own lights⁹.

The fight mattered less than what the dead carried. Two of the sappers had a hand-drawn plan of the compound marked in Vietnamese. It showed the two-storey building of the C3 operations directorate and its plans cell, the generator, the cryptographic room behind the C2 directorate, and the gap in the inner wall's lighting beside the motor pool. The plan was accurate to within a few metres, and the gap had existed only since the generator was moved in November 1967⁹. Whoever drew it had walked the compound within the previous ten weeks.

The investigation of February 1968, run jointly by the Military Security Service and the combined command's American counter-intelligence detachment, took four months and found the man in June. He was a captain of the C3 plans cell, a graduate of the Dalat staff course in 1965, recruited by his brother-in-law in the Saigon–Gia Dinh Region's military intelligence section in 1962 and placed in the combined staff in 1965. He had passed the enemy the combined staff's quarterly plans for III Corps for about two and a half years, and with them the dates of the transitions between plans. He was arrested on 14 June, tried by court-martial and sentenced to death. The sentence was commuted. In the investigation's report the combined command's counter-intelligence chief wrote that the two-layer plan had protected the operations of 1966–67 better than the staff had believed, and the C3 plans cell's secrets worse⁹. The two-layer plan was extended to every corps area in July 1968, and the Vietnamese staff officers' resentment of it grew with it.
